#25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture.
#89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for
#64 — Mean-payoff games,
#65 — Parity games,
#340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games.
#183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes,
#130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart.

comments.author: mananaysiempre
comments.text:
A couple of notes:
- There’s also the notation 0 for the empty (never, noreturn) type. In addition to matching the number of members, the notations 0 and 1 make sense also as units (neutral elements) of addition and multiplication respectively: 0 + A ≅ A + 0 ≅ A, 1 × A ≅ A × 1 ≅ A in a natural way[1]; and also 0 × A ≅ A × 0 ≅ 0.
- That a constant dependent sum is a product, and a constant dependent product is an exponential, is (undeniably confusing at first but) just[2] the naïve schoolbook definition that A × B = B added to itself A times and A^B = A multiplied by itself B times.
- That a constant dependent product is a function type is just the naïve definition that a function is a table of its values at each input (a tuple, with elements numbered by the possible inputs). A dependent function ( = dependent product), then, is the same thing but the allowable values in each cell of the table vary depending on the cell.
- That the function type is the exponential type is also part of common set-theory notation. For instance, 2^ℕ is a not-infrequent name for the set in the Cantor theorem (subsets of the naturals).

This is interesting, although the “beyond specialized models” feels a bit premature. It seems like GPT can act like a glue layer between the highly specialized models that carry out each specific sub-task in a protein design workflow… and in some cases, can outperform specialized models at those tasks.
I’ve noticed that LLMs are very good at this type of glue work between highly specialized fields. It used to be quite difficult to “connect” your own work to adjacent tools made by other SMEs, sometimes so difficult that it was impractical.
I suspect one of the biggest impacts of LLMs on science will be the enablement of more frictionless collaboration and higher-level integration of specialized capabilities in a single study.

stories.title_en: When in Doubt, Flail About

comments.author: FinnLobsien
comments.text:
Reality isn't deterministic. Everyone rationally understands this, but most people don't act on it.
It's foolish to believe that the quality of one's results scales linearly with planning, strategizing, and so on. We've all made intricate plans that went nowhere and done off-the-cuff things that became breakthroughs.
I think the important mental model here is expected value:
What's the potential upside and downside and what probability do I assign to those outcomes?
For everything you do, you should be able to make a credible case that it could lead to a great outcome, but don't bet everything on one scenario.
This creates the mental space to not pick favorites among approaches and act on real results (vs. insisting on the solution that was so elegant in your head).
"Flailing" (I'd call it tinkering) falls apart in two scenarios:
-When one attempt's failure doesn't take you back where you started, but makes you significantly worse off (e.g. larges-scale production infrastructure)
-When the feedback loop isn't based on the results you're trying to achieve (e.g. users like your feature, but an exec doesn't, so the exec deprecates it)

stories.title_en: A faster algorithm for extracting hexadecimal digits of π

comments.author: nickcw
comments.text:
The main boxed formula is equivalent to this Machin style formula for pi
pi = 4 arctan 4/7 + 4 arctan 1/8 + 2 arctan 8/31 + 2 arctan 1/32
Because each of the denominators in the arctans is a power or 2 or 1 different from a power of 2, we can make a BBP formula from it to calculate any hex digit of pi without calculating the previous ones.
I wrote a reasonably accessible account of how this works in
https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/euleriana/vol3/iss1/3/
(which is referenced in the article!)
The boxed formula is exciting because it has been rearranged so that it has a single common denominator, so only needs 1 division per term.
It is the divisions which are slow so reducing the number of them speeds up the calculation. That plus another trick makes the calculation run 40% faster than the best known BBP formula.
> There’s a choice hiding in the last step of Bellard’s terse derivation.
That made me laugh. It took me several days to figure out Bellard's terse derivation :-)

comments.author: Tiberium
comments.text:
For the general picture: the Xbox version of the game was leaked by Cyberleek - first the resources, then the game binary.
Because modern Xbox is very close to a Windows PC with some extra Xbox stuff, running the actual game code isn't hard, it's mostly about compatibility and graphics, plus the binary doesn't have any special DRM/obfuscation.
The current projects (xcl and VIctory) basically take a Wine-like approach. The main problems they have to solve, as I understand:
- The game ships with raw RDNA 2 shaders, so the projects have to translate that to another format, e.g. DXIL for DirectX 12, and compile those shaders. So you need a good translation/recompilation pipeline, if it's bad, the shaders will be bloated and perform poorly
- Xbox has unified memory, while most PCs do not, so you have to add a lot of workarounds and book-keeping for the game to work properly with that
- Xbox's DirectX 12 differs from the normal Windows one in some ways, and the game uses Xbox-specific texture formats with DirectStorage

I heard an interesting question once: if we consider all the greatest discoveries of mankind and imagine a counterfactual world where their discoverer had not existed, how many additional years would it have taken for someone else to have made the discovery?
Subjectively, I think most of the major discoveries would have only been delayed by a decade or two. E.g., general relativity, quantum mechanics, the laws of thermodynamics.
For the incompleteness theorems, however, I’m not sure that we would even be aware of them today without Gödel. Tarski might have come the closest, but there were still a few insane conceptual leaps that had to be made beyond the undefinability of truth.
The theorems are often considered a curiosity at the edges of mathematics, but I’m not so sure. I think they might be more fundamental than typically given credit for. The problem is that the theorems aren’t really actionable since they rule out essentially all algorithmic methods of working around the limitations they entail.
